tldr: To prevent collisions during manipulator teleoperation, the authors proposed "PARRY," a lightweight collision avoidance method that deflects only the direction of relative velocity using Rodrigues' rotation formula while preserving its magnitude, and compensates for perception latency via TTC-based point-cloud prediction.
hero_caption: Concept of PARRY in robotic teleoperation. In the top row, network latency delays evasive action and leads to a collision. In the bottom row with PARRY, the system anticipates the approaching obstacle from camera point clouds and smoothly deflects the end-effector velocity vector for a safe detour.
overview:
Robotic teleoperation is a powerful approach that keeps humans out of harm's way while enabling dexterous manipulation. However, human operators engrossed in tasks often fail to spot suddenly appearing obstacles in time. Even if they notice them and attempt evasive maneuvers, the combination of communication and point-cloud processing latency often makes it impossible to prevent collisions.

To tackle this problem, the authors developed "PARRY," a lightweight collision avoidance framework that intervenes directly at the end-effector velocity-command level. It features two core ideas. First, instead of simply adding force vectors like conventional artificial potential field (APF) methods, it uses Rodrigues' rotation formula to deflect only the direction of the relative velocity while strictly preserving its magnitude. This fundamentally resolves the deadlock problem where attractive and repulsive forces cancel each other out, halting the end-effector. Second, it adaptively predicts future point clouds based on time-to-collision (TTC), allowing safe and proactive evasion even in the presence of pipeline latency.

In simulation, 21,000 Monte Carlo trials across communication latencies of 0 ms, 100 ms, and 150 ms against incoming obstacles demonstrated that PARRY outperforms baseline APF and Control Barrier Function (CBF) methods in collision avoidance success rate. Physical experiments with a 7-DoF robotic manipulator further confirmed that the system can smoothly bypass obstacles in real time while an operator stacks paper cups.
contributions: Proposed "PARRY," a plug-and-play collision avoidance framework for teleoperation that directly modifies end-effector velocity commands without altering lower-level controllers.

Eliminated the velocity stalling (deadlock) common in conventional artificial potential field methods by rotating only the direction of relative velocity with Rodrigues' rotation formula while preserving its magnitude.
Integrated adaptive TTC-based point-cloud prediction with an overshoot protection mechanism to achieve stable collision avoidance under pipeline latency.

Demonstrated superior collision avoidance performance and an extremely fast computation time of 0.101 ms—readily supporting 100 Hz control—through 21,000 simulation trials and physical experiments on a 7-DoF manipulator.

sections.heading: Why Perception Latency and Velocity Deadlock Threaten Safe Teleoperation
sections.summary: In teleoperation, abrupt environmental changes combined with communication and processing latency create serious collision risks. Because existing potential field methods easily stall and control barrier functions face high computational burdens on raw point clouds, this paper proposes PARRY, a lightweight framework that avoids obstacles by steering relative velocity.
sections.details:
Recent advances in teleoperation have enabled robotic manipulators to perform human-arm-like dexterous motions, yet ensuring safety remains a major challenge. When operators focus intently on delicate tasks, they can easily miss suddenly appearing obstacles. Even when they attempt evasive actions, communication delays and multi-stage point-cloud processing pipelines mean the command reaches the physical arm too late.

Various safety-assistance approaches have been studied to address these issues, such as Virtual Fixtures (VF), Control Barrier Functions (CBF), and Artificial Potential Fields (APF). However, VFs are difficult to configure in unknown environments, and solving CBF optimization problems online over raw point clouds imposes a heavy computational load. On the other hand, the more accessible APF method suffers from a critical drawback: attractive forces toward the goal and repulsive forces from obstacles frequently cancel out. This drops the end-effector velocity close to zero, trapping the robot in local minima (deadlocks). When a robot suddenly freezes during teleoperation, operators often suspect a network disconnection or hardware failure, leading them to apply excessive inputs that heighten safety risks.

To overcome these hurdles, the paper proposes PARRY (Predictive Avoidance by Rotating Relative velocitY). PARRY is a lightweight module that operates directly at the end-effector velocity-command level, integrating cleanly without altering underlying tracking controllers. It estimates time-to-collision (TTC) from obstacle motion to project future point-cloud positions and uses Rodrigues' rotation formula to alter only the heading of the relative velocity without changing its magnitude, smoothly steering around obstacles without stalling.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of PARRY. In standard teleoperation (top), latency leads to a collision with a column. In PARRY (bottom), the system predicts the obstacle from camera point clouds and rotates the end-effector velocity direction to track a safe green detour trajectory.

sections.heading: Rotation-Based Avoidance and Latency Compensation: Where PARRY Fits
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes its approach along two main research lineages: geometric rotation of repulsive vectors to overcome potential field stagnation, and predictive compensation for communication and processing latency in teleoperation.
sections.details:
This section organizes related work into two distinct streams.

The first stream is rotation-based obstacle avoidance. To prevent local minima and oscillations in APF, researchers have long explored tangential forces and vortex vector fields around obstacles. Examples include circulatory field methods, magnetic-field-inspired approaches, and superimposed vortex fields created by rotating repulsive fields. Other techniques apply modulation matrices while preserving dynamical system attractors, or rotate 2D navigation trajectories using visual repulsion (such as CARE). However, extending these concepts to 3D dynamic environments under continuously shifting human teleoperation inputs is not straightforward.

The second stream is latency compensation and prediction in teleoperation. To handle communication delays, classic approaches have utilized Smith predictors to estimate delay-free local states, or model-mediated teleoperation that builds contact models of the environment to provide instant haptic feedback. More recently, shared-control schemes have used Model Predictive Control (MPC) to propagate states forward to the current time. Nevertheless, lightweight geometric methods that compensate for multi-stage point-cloud perception delays within a high-frequency velocity control loop have remained largely unaddressed. PARRY bridges this gap by unifying latency compensation and rotational avoidance directly from 3D point clouds with minimal computational overhead.

sections.heading: Inside PARRY: Point-Cloud Prediction and Rodrigues' Velocity Rotation
sections.summary: After filtering self-robot points from the raw depth cloud, PARRY estimates TTC from the most hazardous point to project future point clouds. It then takes the resulting repulsive force as an axis and uses Rodrigues' rotation formula to smoothly steer the relative velocity vector.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and algorithm of PARRY consist of three main stages.

### III-A & III-B: System Overview and Point-Cloud Preprocessing
Let $\mathbf{v}_{ee}$ denote the target end-effector velocity generated by operator input, and $\mathbf{x}_{ee}$ denote the end-effector position. Depth point clouds from an external camera are transformed into the base frame, followed by workspace cropping and voxel downsampling. A self-filtering step removes points inside capsule approximations of the robot's own arm links, and statistical outlier removal yields the obstacle point cloud $\mathcal{O}$.

### III-C: Adaptive Prediction with Overshoot Protection
To cancel out pipeline latency in teleoperation, PARRY predicts future point clouds inspired by time-to-collision (TTC). It first identifies the most critical point closest to the end-effector and estimates obstacle velocity $\mathbf{v}_o$ from inter-frame differences, smoothed with a moving average. Based on this velocity and the approach speed toward the end-effector, an approach time $T_{\mathrm{app}}$ is computed to adaptively set the prediction horizon $t_p$. The displacement $\Delta\mathbf{o} = \mathbf{v}_o t_p$ is added across the point cloud to project future locations. However, shifting all points by the same offset can cause predicted points to overshoot past the end-effector, generating repulsive forces in the opposite direction. To prevent this, an overshoot protection mechanism clamps each point so it does not breach a minimum safety distance $d_s$, while resetting points that have already moved away from the end-effector.

### III-D: Safe Velocity Generation via Rodrigues' Rotation
From each point in the predicted cloud $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}$, a power-law repulsive force is computed and distance-weighted to obtain the net repulsive force $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{rep}}$. Directly adding this force to the velocity command, as in conventional APF, would cause mutual cancellation and stall the robot. Instead, PARRY calculates the relative velocity in the obstacle frame, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rel}} = \mathbf{v}_{ee} - \mathbf{v}_o$, and determines a rotation axis $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$ from the cross product of $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ and $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{rep}}$.
Using Rodrigues' rotation formula, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is rotated by a deflection angle $\theta$ proportional to the repulsive force magnitude. The key advantage is that the norm of the relative velocity remains completely unchanged; only its direction deflects away from the obstacle. In singular cases where velocity and repulsion are antiparallel, PARRY preserves the previous frame's rotation axis to slip past the obstacle without freezing. Finally, the obstacle velocity is added back to output the commanded velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$ in the base frame.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of PARRY. The upper pipeline preprocesses the depth point cloud and generates a predicted point cloud via TTC. The lower pipeline deflects relative velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ via Rodrigues' rotation in the obstacle frame to produce the final velocity command $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$.

sections.heading: Proven in 21,000 Trials: Superior Avoidance and No Deadlocks
sections.summary: Across 21,000 MuJoCo simulations with incoming spherical obstacles under 0 ms, 100 ms, and 150 ms latencies, PARRY achieved the highest collision avoidance rates across all delay settings and confirmed the complete absence of APF-style velocity stalls.
sections.details:
Simulation experiments were conducted in MuJoCo using a UR5e manipulator equipped with a Robotiq gripper. While executing pick-and-place trajectories mimicking operator commands, spherical obstacles of 0.10 m radius were launched at 0.5–3.5 m/s toward a 0.25 m radius region around the end-effector from a distance of roughly 1.5 m. Gaussian noise was added to point positions and velocities, and three latency settings were evaluated: $\tau = 0, 100, 150$ ms. Exactly 1,000 random seeds were evaluated per latency, under identical conditions for all baselines.

### IV-C 1 & 2: Baseline Comparison and Latency Robustness
PARRY was compared against three baselines: APF-VS (which adds APF repulsive forces directly), CBF-QP (Control Barrier Functions), and SSM (Speed and Separation Monitoring per international standards). At 0 ms delay, PARRY reduced the collision rate by 17.2% compared to APF-VS, 27.3% compared to CBF-QP, and 38.7% compared to SSM (all $p < 0.01$ via McNemar tests).
When latency increased to 150 ms, the collision rate degraded by 5.4 percentage points for APF-VS and 4.3 percentage points for CBF-QP, whereas PARRY degraded by only 2.6 percentage points. As latency grows, the prediction module proves its value, showing noticeably milder performance degradation than the baselines.

### IV-C 3: Ablation Studies
To evaluate individual components, ablations were tested against the full PARRY. Compared to omitting the relative velocity formulation (w/o Rel), including relative velocity reduced the collision rate by 23.2%. Adding point-cloud prediction to a model without it (w/o Pred) reduced the collision rate at 150 ms latency by 24.9%. While overshoot protection (Guard) had only a modest impact on the raw collision rate, it drastically reduced repulsive force direction flips (changes $>90^\circ$) from 20.2% to 3.6% and almost eradicated reverse repulsive forces from 20.4% down to 0.1%, eliminating unnatural control artifacts.

### IV-C 4 & 5: Computation Time and Local Minima Avoidance
The median minimum clearance between the end-effector and the obstacle surface was highest for PARRY at 0.188 m (versus 0.150 m for APF-VS and 0.135 m for CBF-QP), offering a larger safety margin. The median computation time was an exceptionally fast 0.101 ms—far lighter than CBF-QP's 0.729 ms—easily fitting within a 100 Hz control loop.
Furthermore, in an environment with two symmetric spheres prone to local minima, APF-VS suffered severe forward-velocity oscillations near zero, causing the arm to stall and form a prolonged plateau. In contrast, PARRY preserved its forward velocity component and smoothly navigated between the obstacles to reach the goal much faster.

captions.F6: Profiles of end-effector forward velocity $v_y$ (top) and position $y$ (bottom) when passing between two symmetric obstacles. Dashed APF-VS stalls near zero velocity upon entering the influence zone, while solid PARRY sustains forward velocity and slips through smoothly.

sections.heading: Real-Time Validation with a Physical Arm and VR Controller
sections.summary: Tested on a 7-DoF Flexiv Rizon 4 arm controlled via Meta Quest 3 controllers during a cup-stacking task, PARRY successfully demonstrated automatic real-time end-effector detours around both static obstacles and dynamic obstacles introduced mid-motion.
sections.details:
To verify performance with a real human in the control loop, the authors evaluated PARRY on a physical robotic testbed.

The system comprised a 7-DoF collaborative robot, the Flexiv Rizon 4, with operators commanding target end-effector poses using Meta Quest 3 VR controllers. An Intel RealSense D435 depth camera positioned in front of the workspace captured point clouds at 30 Hz. A local workstation executed PARRY's preprocessing, prediction, and velocity deflection routines at a 100 Hz control cycle, feeding corrected velocity commands directly to the robot's low-level controller.

The experimental task required grasping four randomly oriented paper cups one by one, neatly stacking them on the opposite side, and then returning them to their initial locations. Because irregular cup orientations demand precise alignment, this task requires human teleoperation rather than fully autonomous execution.

In a static obstacle scenario with a milk carton placed along the transit route, normal teleoperation led to a collision that knocked the carton over. With PARRY active, even when the operator attempted to drive the cup straight through, the end-effector automatically lifted upward to bypass the carton, completing the stack without disruption. In a dynamic scenario where an obstacle was manually thrust into the path during transport, the system also executed evasive maneuvers in real time, confirming practical responsiveness on real hardware.

captions.F7: Comparison of static obstacle avoidance on the physical robot. In the baseline (top), the arm collides with a milk carton in the path. With PARRY (bottom), velocity command $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$ rotates upward by deflection angle $\theta$, smoothly vaulting over the obstacle.
captions.F8: 3D trajectories from physical experiments. The blue line is the operator's reference trajectory, the red line is the actual end-effector path $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ee}}$, and green points represent the obstacle. Even with straight operator inputs, the arm smoothly routes upward before the obstacle.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Expanding Toward Whole-Arm Safety
sections.summary: PARRY is a lightweight collision avoidance method that overcomes teleoperation-specific latency and velocity stagnation by pairing TTC prediction with Rodrigues-based relative velocity deflection. Future work aims to expand protection from the end-effector to the entire manipulator body.
sections.details:
This paper presented PARRY, a predictive relative-velocity steering approach designed to enhance teleoperation safety for robotic manipulators in dynamic environments. The cornerstone of PARRY is the combination of TTC-based point-cloud prediction, overshoot protection, and Rodrigues' rotation formula to steer relative velocity while preserving its magnitude. This proactive scheme compensates for perception and transmission delays while eliminating the local-minima stalls typical of traditional APF methods.

Rigorous pairwise Monte Carlo simulations (21,000 trials in total) and physical experiments on a 7-DoF manipulator validated its high collision avoidance rate and minimal computational footprint suited for high-rate real-time control. At present, however, the implementation focuses solely on end-effector collision avoidance and does not protect the rest of the arm, such as the elbow or forearm links. The authors highlight extending geometric constraints to all manipulator links and quantitatively assessing the impact of safety interventions on operator workload and task completion time as key future directions.

takeaways: When applying potential field methods to teleoperation, steering velocity vectors while preserving their norm—rather than naively summing forces—effectively prevents stalls and deadlocks.
Adaptive TTC-based point-cloud prediction effectively mitigates teleoperation pipeline latency, substantially curbing performance drop-offs even at delays up to 150 ms.
Projecting entire point clouds forward can cause points to overshoot past the end-effector and invert repulsive forces; clamping them with overshoot protection is essential for behavioral stability.
At 0.101 ms, computation is more than an order of magnitude faster than optimization-based CBFs, making it seamless to plug into control loops running at 100 Hz or higher.
limitations: Collision avoidance is currently limited to the end-effector, leaving arm links such as the elbow vulnerable to contact with obstacles.
The quantitative impact of automated velocity steering on operator cognitive load, perceived naturalness, and task completion time has not yet been evaluated with human subjects.
